app:impl.source_text: \section{Implementation details: shallow circuits and fixed-scale networks}

c-abstract.source_text: \begin{abstract} Why can neural networks struggle to learn optimal play in a game with a simple, efficient solution algorithm? Motivated by empirical difficulties with parity in impartial games, we use NIM to study a representational bottleneck and three ways around it. We show that a restricted model of shallow, fixed-scale quantised networks lies in $\AC^0$, a circuit class unable to compute parity on arbitrarily large inputs. This prevents optimal single-position play across all board sizes within the model. The obstruction also guides architectural design: two-frame inputs allow restoration from a known zero-nim-sum position; complementary rollout policies reveal the missing invariant; and persistent recurrence accumulates it row by row. Each route retains shallow network components while supplying additional information or processing time. Supervised experiments illustrate the benefits of two-frame restoration and multiple rollout heads; recurrence is a theoretical construction. These results establish representational possibilities, not guarantees of successful training: $\AC^0$ does not characterise practical learnability. Core mathematical results and constructions have been checked in Lean, with classical complexity results as explicit external inputs. The interactive edition and complete Lean sources are available online \citep{riis2026interactive,riis2026lean}. \end{abstract}

c-arbitrary-starts.source_text: Allowing arbitrary start positions would defeat the single-channel restriction: querying $\pi_0$ on heaps consisting of the $k$th bits of $P$ returns $\sigma_k(P)$. Likewise, an unrestricted sequential controller could compute the nim-sum itself. The lower bound therefore concerns the stated measurement/readout model, not general MCTS or all single-policy algorithms.

c-author-verification-scope.source_text: The author's review of the formalisation focused on the interface between the paper and Lean: whether the formal definitions, hypotheses and conclusions express the intended mathematical claims. The author did not manually inspect every theorem or lemma declaration or every line of Lean source. Mechanical checking verifies the formal proofs relative to their definitions and stated hypotheses; it does not independently certify the correspondence with the prose, the suitability of the modelling assumptions, or the experimental results.

c-baseline-arith.source_text: \emph{Single-head baseline.} The single-head baseline achieves 0.768~overall accuracy and 0.536~N-position recall. These numbers have an exact theoretical explanation. With $k=4$ bits, an N-position has nim-sum $\sigma \in \{1,\dots,15\}$. Of these 15~values, exactly~8 are odd ($\sigma_0 = 1$: the values $1,3,5,7,9,11,13,15$) and 7~are even ($\sigma_0 = 0$). Head~$\pi_0$ detects an N-position only when $\sigma_0 = 1$, so the theoretical N-position recall is $8/15 \approx 0.533$ (observed: 0.536 on the finite test set). All P-positions are correctly classified (since $\sigma = 0$ implies $\sigma_0 = 0$), so on a balanced test set the overall accuracy is $\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{8}{15} = \tfrac{23}{30} \approx 0.767$ (observed: 0.768). This calculation describes the particular classifier that declares an N-position exactly when $r_0=1$. It is not the winning-move success bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:search-gap}(i), and does not establish a limit on arbitrary classifiers or rollout policies.

c-benchmark-evaluation.source_text: These are proposed learning challenges, not consequences of the present $\AC^0$ lower bound. An unresolved structural question is not itself a complexity lower bound, and worst-case hardness need not make a chosen instance distribution difficult. A useful evaluation would reserve unseen sizes and positions, report both training and decision-time computation, and compare play with exact solvers where feasible and strong search baselines elsewhere. Beyond the range of exact verification, improved win rates are evidence of stronger play rather than a solution of an open mathematical problem. The central question is whether self-play discovers reusable strategic structure that extends the range of positions it can handle under a fixed computation budget.

c-binary-index.source_text: Let $s_i$ be the candidate flags after choosing between cancellation and fallback. More than one may be true. Define \[ f_i=s_i\wedge\bigwedge_{j<i}\neg s_j, \qquad I_k=\bigvee_{\substack{0\le i<N\\\text{bit }k\text{ of }i\text{ is }1}}f_i. \] The $f_i$ flags select the first candidate; the $I_k$ wires give its binary index. Masking the candidate replacement bits by $f_i$ and taking OR gives the value output. Combining validity with $\bigvee_i s_i$ handles the absence of candidates. This uses constant additional depth and polynomial size, rather than an uncosted external search for the first true flag. The Lean priority encoder proves agreement for every flag pattern, including invalid outputs, no candidates, and the cases $N=0$ and $N=1$. A move index uses $r$ bits with $N\le2^r$; the replay counter also stores $N$ and therefore requires $N<2^r$.

c-board-storage.source_text: Computing $\sigma_t$ does not by itself retain the heap rows needed to choose a move. One implementation replays the current position after the first scan. If $\sigma_t\ne0$, select the first row $i$ for which \[ x_{t,i}'=x_{t,i}\oplus\sigma_t<x_{t,i}. \] Such a row exists: choose a heap containing the highest set bit of $\sigma_t$. Replacing that heap by $x_{t,i}'$ leaves nim-sum zero. XOR, binary comparison and conditional selection are constant-depth operations; the replay uses $O(B+\log N)$ state bits to retain the summary, a selected move and its row index. The explicit protocol is \[ \mathtt{rows}(P_t),\ \mathtt{SEP},\ \mathtt{rows}(P_t),\ \mathtt{SEP}. \] The first separator stores the summary and switches to replay; the second emits the move and returns to scan mode. This takes exactly $2N+2$ updates, with one additional reset token at the start of a game. If $\sigma_t=0$, choose the first nonempty heap and decrement it, or report termination when all heaps are empty. Lean verifies the complete replay controller, including its binary move output and its fixed-scale threshold implementation. With an $r$-bit counter satisfying $N<2^r$, its state uses $4+5B+3r$ bits. The strict inequality allows the counter to hold the end value $N$, whereas an output index alone only needs $N\le2^r$. Alternatively, store the current board in $O(NB)$ bits during the initial scan and use a constant-depth selector at the separator, as in Appendix~\ref{app:impl}. This avoids replay at the cost of board-sized memory. The distinction matters for a stream in which each position is supplied only once. Both variants have checked bit-level circuits, fixed-scale network implementations and winning-play guarantees. The board-storage variant uses $NB+B+r$ state bits and $N+1$ updates per decision, with $N<2^r$, plus a reset update when initialising the controller.

c-bypass-not-ac0.source_text: These are three ways around the \emph{same restricted inference problem}, not three shallow algorithms for unrestricted parity. The two-frame construction changes the input and imposes a promise. The other constructions allow processing time to grow. Their complete board-to-winning-move maps cannot themselves form an $\AC^0$ family: otherwise applying either to $(2,b_1,\ldots,b_m)$ would contradict Theorem~\ref{thm:singleframe-impossible}. Parallel output heads alone do not supply the rollout computation, and separators alone do not supply a recurrent scan. Appendix~\ref{app:impl} illustrates the explicit network constructions and explains their conservative depth and layer bounds.

c-candidate-moves.source_text: On a legal transition only one heap changes. Consequently, bit $k$ of the delta is \[ \delta_k=\bigvee_{i=0}^{N-1}(x_{i,k}\oplus x'_{i,k}). \] The single-change promise makes OR equal to the required XOR across changed rows. For a target $\delta$ supplied as input bits, form $y_i=x_i\oplus\delta$ in parallel. The test $y_i<x_i$ is shallow: OR over the possible highest differing bit, requiring equality at every higher bit and $y_{i,k}=0,x_{i,k}=1$ at that bit. Each test has size polynomial in $B$. When no cancelling candidate exists, use the first nonzero heap and subtract one. Bit $k$ of that decrement is $x_{i,k}$ XOR the conjunction saying that all lower bits are zero. The validity bit is false exactly when the board is terminal. In restoration, the target comes from the two-frame delta; in the multi-head readout it comes from reconstruction of the rollout outcomes.

c-conclusion.source_text: \label{sec:conclusion} A fixed-depth Boolean literal-threshold model with nonnegative fixed-grid weights and bounded thresholds is simulable in $\AC^0$. The NIM parity reduction then rules out strong single-frame mastery in that model.

c-conclusion-bypasses.source_text: Three constructions identify resources beyond that restricted inference problem. Two-frame access supports constant-depth restoration when the preceding position has nim-sum zero. Distinct structured rollout policies reveal complementary invariant bits; a single-channel limitation holds only under our explicit query and readout restrictions. Persistent recurrence implements running XOR over heap rows, exchanging fixed total latency for a growing sequence of simple updates. Cross-position memory additionally supports comparisons, while replay or board storage supplies the heaps needed for move selection.

c-conclusion-experiments.source_text: The saved floating-point experiments show a large supervised two-frame restoration advantage and perfect finite-test $P/N$ classification by a learned multi-head controller. The latter coexists with imperfect individual channel recovery. The restoration plateaus and checkpoint diagnostics also show that learning can proceed in stages after transition information is supplied. These observations do not certify the formal gate assumptions, worst-case mastery, or self-play discovery.

c-condorcet.source_text: \label{sec:math} Exposing local invariants may also help guide combinatorial search. Our work on large Condorcet domains used structural constructions and local restrictions \citep{karpov2023setalternating,zhou2024cdl,zhou2024phd}. This is a motivating analogy, not an $\AC^0$ reduction or a demonstrated parity lower bound for that search problem. Transferring the present argument requires a precisely encoded computational task.

c-contributions.source_text: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item \textbf{$\AC^0$ containment for fixed-scale quantised inference.} We formalise a fixed-grid Boolean literal-threshold model and its bounded-unrolling recurrent extension. Both are simulable by $\AC^0$ circuits (Theorem~\ref{thm:sim-ac0}). An attention-style extension is covered only when all its operations have an explicit implementation in the same permitted gates. \item \textbf{Single-frame impossibility for strong mastery.} Under this model, no single-frame policy/value network can strongly master NIM in the worst case (Theorem~\ref{thm:singleframe-impossible}). \item \textbf{Two-frame bypass via local differences and restoration.} With two consecutive frames, the agent can compute $\Delta(P,P')$ in $\AC^0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:nimber-diff-ac0}). When $P$ has nim-sum zero, an $\AC^0$ move selector restores zero after the opponent's move (Proposition~\ref{prop:restore}). This is conditional restoration mastery, not an arbitrary-start verifier. \item \textbf{Planning analysis and the single-policy bottleneck.} We analyse a restricted measurement interface inspired by rollouts, rather than a general model of MCTS. With $B$ structured policies one can recover all nim-sum bits (Proposition~\ref{prop:rollout-sufficiency}). Root and one-heap-modification queries to one fixed member of that family expose only one unknown linear functional (Proposition~\ref{prop:single-policy-bound}). With an explicitly bounded readout, this yields the distributional bound in Theorem~\ref{thm:search-gap}. \item \textbf{Persistent recurrence via sequential row updates.} A constant-depth recurrent update accumulates the nim-sum over $N$ heap rows and retains a summary across position separators (Proposition~\ref{prop:streaming-nimsum}). With a replay of the current board or stored heap rows, this supports optimal move selection. The construction relaxes fixed total latency, not fixed-scale quantisation (Section~\ref{sec:recurrent-bypass}). \item \textbf{Controlled empirical comparison and learnability discussion.} On 20-heap, 4-bit NIM with $10^6$ supervised restoration examples, a one-frame model has low restoration accuracy while a two-frame model learns restoration (Section~\ref{sec:supervised-restoration}). In a complementary single-frame experiment, multi-head FSM-controlled shootouts achieve perfect win/loss position classification while the single-head baseline remains bottlenecked by one-bit information (Section~\ref{sec:exp-fsm-shootout}). We also discuss why $\AC^0$ is a useful abstraction for what is robustly feasible under fixed-scale quantised inference (Section~\ref{sec:majority-vs-parity}). \end{itemize}

c-controller-evals.source_text: Let $M$ be the total number of simulated legal moves in the all-head schedule. The implementation uses $M+2B+2$ component evaluations: $M$ move updates, $B$ terminal tests, $B$ outcome-consumption updates, one initial reset and one final move readout. Since $M\le BN(2^B-1)$, this agrees with the rollout-time bound in the main text while making the control overhead explicit. These are circuit evaluations, not measured processor time. The early-exit schedule uses only the visited heads and gives the same classification as the OR of all outcomes. These certificates concern the two specified schedules; the abstract definition of a finite-state controller does not certify arbitrary scheduling logic.

c-delta-local.source_text: In NIM, if $P'$ is obtained from $P$ by changing heap $i$ from $x_i$ to $x_i'$, then \[ \Delta(P,P') \;=\; x_i \oplus x_i', \] a purely local computation on the changed heap.

c-depth-amplification.source_text: Although a single $\AC^0$ circuit cannot compute parity, iterating an $\AC^0$ policy for $L$ game steps yields an effective depth $\Theta(L)$ computation, which can reveal parity information. The next proposition makes this explicit by exhibiting $B$ simple $\AC^0$ rollout heads whose outcomes recover all $B$ bits of the nim-sum.
