thm:nim-win.source_text: \begin{theorem}[Classical NIM characterisation] \label{thm:nim-win} A NIM position $(x_1,\dots,x_h)$ is losing for the player to move iff $\operatorname{nim}(x_1,\dots,x_h)=0$. Moreover, from any winning position (nim-sum $\neq 0$) there is a move to a losing position (nim-sum $=0$). \end{theorem}

thm:search-gap.i.source_text: \begin{theorem}[Restricted bound and bypasses] \label{thm:search-gap} The following statements hold under Definition~\ref{def:agent-types}. \begin{enumerate} \item[\textup{(i)}] For each fixed $B\ge2$, let $P$ be uniform on $\{0,\ldots,2^B-1\}^N$ conditional on $\sigma(P)\ne0$. For one fixed structured head $\pi_j$ and an $\AC^0$ readout $F_N(P,\mathrm{RO}_{\pi_j}(P))$, winning-move success is at most \[ \frac{2}{2^B-1}+\operatorname{negl}(N). \] Here $N\ge1$, and a negligible error is a nonnegative sequence smaller than every inverse polynomial for sufficiently large $N$, with circuit depth, polynomial size exponent and $B$ fixed. More precisely, a uniform parity-correlation bound $\eta_N$ for the fixed-bit readout indicators gives the finite upper bound $2/(2^B-1)+(2^B-1)\eta_N$; the indicators and correlation premise are specified in Appendix~\ref{app:search-gap-proof}. The leading constant is asymptotically attainable by guessing one nonzero nim-sum in each channel fibre. \item[\textup{(ii)}] For any $B$, the $B$ structured heads and an $\AC^0$ readout select an optimal move using $O(BN2^B)$ rollout steps, as in Proposition~\ref{prop:rollout-sufficiency}. \item[\textup{(iii)}] Given a legal transition from a known zero-nim-sum predecessor, a two-frame $\AC^0$ selector restores zero. Once a player has established that invariant, it maintains it against every legal opponent response. This statement does not supply the initial winning move from an arbitrary position. \end{enumerate} \end{theorem}

thm:sim-ac0.source_text: \begin{theorem}[Simulation by $\AC^0$] \label{thm:sim-ac0} Fix constants $W,D\in\N$ and a time window $T\in\N$. Let $\{\mathcal{M}_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ be any family of models of type $\NN$, $\RNN$ (with window $T$), or $\LTST$ (with window $T$) such that: \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,label=(\arabic*)] \item (\textbf{Polynomial size}) the number of neurons/units in $\mathcal{M}_n$ is at most $\poly(n)$. \item (\textbf{Constant depth}) the number of layers is a fixed constant $L$ (independent of $n$); for $\RNN/\LTST$ the entire unrolled computation uses at most $T$ time steps from an input-independent initial state. \item (\textbf{Permitted primitives}) every operation is realised by the Boolean literal-threshold gates of Definition~\ref{def:NN-formal}; all weights and thresholds lie in $\Qset_{W,D}$. For the attention-style extension this includes score computation, coefficient selection and aggregation. \end{enumerate} Then the Boolean function computed by $\mathcal{M}_n$ can be computed by an $\AC^0$ circuit family of polynomial size and constant depth (depending only on $L,T,W,D$). \end{theorem}

thm:singleframe-impossible.a.source_text: \begin{theorem}[Single-frame parity barrier] \label{thm:singleframe-impossible} Consider the restricted family of NIM positions $P(\mathbf{b})=(2,b_1,\dots,b_m)$ where $b_i\in\{0,1\}$. Any single-frame agent that achieves strong mastery must compute the parity $b_1\oplus\cdots\oplus b_m$. Since $\mathrm{PARITY}\notin \AC^0$, no polynomial-size, constant-depth fixed-scale quantised network can strongly master NIM. \end{theorem}

x-example-pairing-strategy.source_text: \begin{example}[Pairing strategy] Consider positions $(a,a,b,b,c,c,\dots)$ consisting of pairs of equal heaps. The second player can mirror the first player’s move on the matching heap, maintaining the paired structure until termination, hence winning. The checked binary selector finds the first unequal pair and reduces its larger heap to match its partner. It has constant depth and polynomial size, and wins against every legal opponent from the paired family when playing second. For the first-player role every paired initial board is losing, so weak mastery there would be vacuous. \end{example}

x-remark-negations.source_text: \begin{remark}[Negations] If some inputs are negated before weighting, i.e.\ $(z_j\oplus \eta_j)$, this simply replaces $z_j$ by either $z_j$ or $\neg z_j$ in each conjunction term. Since $\AC^0$ allows NOT gates, Lemma~\ref{lem:unit-ac0} still applies. \end{remark}
